title: Ardas before a journey
hook: before travel, exams or new work, Sikhs ask for help in Ardas

segments.voice: Yesterday, karah prashad, and your line: thanks before food. Did you pause before a bite? Today the Ardas walks out the front door with you. Day six hundred forty.

The suitcase is zipped. The car is running in the driveway, or the ride is two minutes away. A student has an exam at nine. Someone is starting a new job on Monday and hasn't slept well all weekend. In some Sikh families, before anyone walks out, there's a moment. Hands fold. A short Ardas is said, sometimes by a grandparent, sometimes by the traveler. Sometimes the family goes to the gurdwara first and asks for the Ardas there. Then, and only then, the door opens.
screen: `THE SUITCASE IS ZIPPED.` → `AN EXAM AT NINE.` → `HANDS FOLD BEFORE THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Every full Ardas already asks for this. Near the end comes the line sarbat de kaaraj raas karne: make everyone's tasks succeed. Kaaraj is a task, a piece of work, an undertaking. Raas means set right, brought to a good end. It's a general request, for everybody. Before a journey, an exam, a wedding, a surgery or a new business, Sikhs make it specific: this trip, this test, this first day. Families sometimes offer karah prashad at the gurdwara so the Ardas can be said there, with the congregation joining in. There's a line in the Guru Granth Sahib that fits these moments. In Sri Rag ki Var, on ang 91, it says, in effect: whatever work you want done, speak of it to the Lord; the True Guru will set it right, and you have His word on it. Notice what this asking is and isn't. It isn't a lucky charm, and it isn't a way to skip the studying. Sikh teaching expects honest effort: you still pack, still prepare, still drive carefully. In the Ardas, effort and outcome come in an order: the work is done, the result is placed in the hands of the One, and then the traveler goes. There's a practical side, too. Saying a task out loud before starting means naming what you're actually walking into. A short Ardas makes it plain: this is the road, this is what I hope for, this is in Your hands.
screen: `SARBAT DE KAARAJ RAAS KARNE.` · `NAME THIS TRIP, THIS TEST.` · `SPEAK OF IT TO THE LORD.` · `EFFORT FIRST, OUTCOME GIVEN.` · then, large: `ASK BEFORE YOU GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a pause at the threshold. Think of your very next real task: a call, a drive, a meeting, a page of homework. Picture the doorway you'll cross to get to it, or the screen you'll open. On the in-breath, picture yourself doing the work honestly and well. On the out-breath, let go of how it turns out. Do that a few times. If you pray, you can place it before the One in your own words, or simply say Waheguru. Then, when the sit ends, begin that task. The bell holds the time.
Kaaraj, a task or undertaking: before travel, exams, new work, Sikhs name it in Ardas and ask that it be brought to a good end, kaaraj raas.
Your line: ask before you go. Today, before you leave the house or start something hard, stop at the door for one breath and name what you're walking into. Day six hundred forty.

howItsDone: Before travel, exams, a new job or another undertaking, Sikhs often say a short Ardas at home or ask for one at the gurdwara, sometimes offering karah prashad, asking that the task be brought to a good end.

fork.setup: you're leaving for a long trip in five minutes. your grandmother stops you at the door. what's she likely to ask?
options: a short Ardas before you go.
fork.reveal: the Ardas doesn't replace packing. the work comes first, then the result is placed in the hands of the One.

original.note: Gurmukhi: a task or undertaking; sarbat de kaaraj raas, may everyone's tasks succeed.

trapdoor: what you thought: praying for good luck.
what it means: naming the task before God and asking that it come to a good end, after doing your part.
what a scholar hears: the general petition sarbat de kaaraj raas karne is made particular for each occasion, echoing Sri Rag ki Var's counsel to bring every task to the Lord.
